entry.title: How I Started My Indieweb Journey
entry.summary: I wrote this post for a prompt given during our local Indieweb club meeting: “Capture the moment that led to starting your blog.” I bought this domain name “abhinavsarkar.net” in June 2007. Sometime during 2006 I joined Twitter, and it opened up a new world to me. Through it, I got introduced to the idea of people having personal websites, and writing on them. entry.title: feed-repeat v1.1: Hosting on GitHub Pages, New Posts Passthrough, SSRF Protection, and More
entry.summary: feed-repeat is a small tool that selects old posts from RSS/Atom feeds you configure and puts them into a new Atom feed. Use it with your feed reader for a spaced-repetition-like experience for feeds. See the announcement post for the motivation behind it, and more details. I just released v1.1 of feed-repeat. This release brings some great new features, and improves the security and performance. The biggest highlight: you can now run feed-repeat entirely on GitHub, no server needed! The repo now includes a GitHub Actions workflow that runs feed-repeat daily, and publishes the generated feeds to GitHub Pages. Getting started is simple: fork the repo, edit config.yaml with your source feeds, enable the workflow, enable GitHub Pages, and subscribe to the generated feeds in your feed reader. …

entry.title: Notes for the Week #23 (2026)
entry.summary:
This week note covers the week of 1st–7th June.
Life# Last week was a week of rest and recovery. I felt better with each passing day. I wonder if what happened to me in the last month was some sort of echo of my burnout and spell of illness of the last year. But this time I didn’t wait six months, I immediately started focusing on resting and nutrition. I hope this cuts down my recovery period substantially. Although I can walk ten thousand steps a day, I’m not forcing myself too, at least for next few weeks. The weather has been fine. I’m sad to miss exercising outside, but resting is a priority for now. I’ll try going to the gym this week. Let’s see. Personal Projects# I stayed indoors, and spent all my free time working on feed-repeat, my recently open-sourced niche Haskell project. One of the things I did was to create a website for it, so now you can read about the work I did right there. I’m very close to a second release. I also upgraded NixOS to version 26.05 on my VPS. I ran into a snag, that I ranted about on internet. IndieWebClub# There was no IWC meetup last week, but a few folks wrote about the Special Edition meetup in their blogs, which was really nice to read about. I also wrote about it, specifically about the behind-the-scenes work we did to make it happen. Watching# Wife and I started watching Spider Noir on Prime Video. It’s a great show but I’m a little disappointed that it’s mostly Noir and very less Spider. I finished watching Bocchi the Rock!. What a great show! It made me start going to music classes again. Interesting Internet Links# Quality in the Age of Slop Thinking about names, as well as scuba diving A Reckless Introduction to Hindley-Milner Type Inference That’s all for this week. You can subscribe to the feed of my week notes for updates.

entry.title: The software industry: annealing, but wrong
entry.summary: In recent months I've heard of several teams with an interesting policy: each pull request should be no more than a few files, and no more than a certain number of lines (say 500). And do just one thing and do it well. And be easy for a human to review. And be fully tested by the test suite. All those are good requirements, right? Surely this is quality software engineering. And often, the results are good. Sure, splitting a single 6000-line feature or fix into twelve 500-line PRs is more work, but each of those PRs is surely easier to review. And you can git bisect them when there's a bug! And maybe revert the individual change that broke something. ...and also cause 12x as many context switches for your reviewers as they review each one sequentially.1 But that's just the cost of software…
